items.text: Agree with Misti Y-- some love Cirque shows and still hate Le Reve. But that's separate. For me the theater and visual design is the strong part. Scenery and decor is breathtaking start to finish, the whole concept is beautiful and appealing. Doesn't translate well to live though. Storyline isn't especially entertaining, stage malfunctioned repeatedly during the one show I went to. Hard to stay engaged even in the impressive scenes. Reaching for that flair and spectacle of Cirque, never quite gets there. Consider it mainly for that beautiful theater experience. Otherwise probably better to spend money on another show.

I paid $38 for this used mechanical keyboard. I think I got about $38 worth maybe a little more. The space bar rattles. Every thumb press gives a hollow clatter, like nudging a tray of cutlery. During the day I tune it out. After midnight I type around it. The E key also repeats now and then. meeting becomes meeeting. Happens once every few paragraphs. Rare enough to forget but frequent enough that I reread everything before hitting send. I messaged the seller asking what switches it used, got tired of waiting, bought it anyway. Answer came a week later, keyboard was already on my desk. Brown switches for the record. The comfort is why I'm keeping it. Each key has a small bump partway down. Fingers know a press registered without slamming to the bottom. Long email done and wrists feel fine afterwards. Laptop keys never managed that. Thought about sending it back. Return shipping would eat a real chunk of what I paid and I'd be back on the laptop. So it stays. Rattle and all.

Saw this in vegas, circus style. Recommend it, minus one star. Story is kinda hard to follow, some music is sleepy or doesnt fit the action. But the performers are wild, serious athletic ability, great physiques, aerobic skills. Female ones are really special, they stay underwater for several minutes. The theater is circular, stage is circular too so every seat has a good view. Three entrances on the stage get used, important at story transitions. Stage, setting and lighting are beautiful, makes a memorable atmosphere. Prices are reasonable vs O or Love. Wanted more spectacle, especially fire, but not a big flaw. Storytelling and music issues aside, its entertaining, visually striking, clearly recommend.

Remote work gets held up as the cure for all ills. Worked with 5 junior engineers for 2 years. Overblown if they are still learning how to code. Jrs do not need tickets or docs or meetings. They need to sit in on design conversations, watch others debug, ask questions before spending hours confused. That interaction happens organically in an office. Remote means they have to know when to cut in, set up calls, explain problems they might not fully understand. That is a tough skill to have before you get a chance to learn it. Seen feedback issues with remote work. Short code review comments feel like final word instead of learning opportunity. Also takes longer so less momentum. The jrs I mentored improved faster with in person pairing, whiteboard sessions, easy access to seniors. Not pushing for offices or anti-flexibility. Remote can be great for self-driven devs. For jrs proximity is a booster, gives confidence, context, instincts. Sending jrs off with laptop and calendar can drag on junior development and result in less good technical leadership later.

317 AM. Industrial mixer humming low steady drone, vibrates through soles of Elias boots. Flour dust in air catches the harsh fluorescent light like suspended snow. Sourdough loaves resting on wooden boards, crusts pale soft before final bake. Wipes hands on apron, fabric stiff with dried dough and sweat. Moves to front counter, checks the lock. Ritual born of paranoia not necessity.

There it sat. The History of Salt. Hardback blue spine cracked near hinge. Appears every Thursday six weeks now, placed precisely on glass display case beside unsold cinnamon rolls. No library stamp, and the bakery is not a branch of municipal system. Picks it up. Cover feels cold. Opens it, expects blank pages or forgotten bookmark. Instead a folded square of lined notebook paper slips out, lands on counter with soft tap. Unfolds. Handwriting jagged, pressed hard into the fiber. Says: you knead with left hand dominant, stop favoring the right, it ruins the tension. Stares at words. Mixer ticks over to next cycle. Looks at own hands, red knuckled dusted white. Closes book. Places it back on glass, aligning spine perfectly with edge. Turns off overhead light above display, leaves book in shadow.

Apple deserves a mention here. My school allowed only apple computers for middle high school students, apple laptops were expensive and cost twice as much as pc alternatives. Machines broke about monthly. Never dropped my laptop but replaced hard drive 5 times in 4 years, reinstalled os many times. One bad case, a friends macbook pro caught fire while he was watching a movie, smoke alarm went off. Apple support couldn't diagnose problems, they just backup the computer, wipe it, restore files. Criticism extends to iphones too. Had the first iphone, frequently malfunctioned. Now apple releases a new iphone about every 2 months with just slightly better camera than previous model. One positive point, qualified, ipads are best tablets currently but android tablets may catch up.

So I went to Awakening at Wynn Las Vegas. It's fine. Not a must see show. Not one of those I'd build a Vegas trip around. I've been to Vegas a lot. As a kid constantly. Saw a ton of shows before I turned 21. So I have a decent baseline for what these productions can be. Good news. The circular stage is smart. Any seat gives a decent view. That's rare in big theater shows. Staying at Wynn or Encore gets you tickets for $99, normally $125. Good deal. Some individual acts are impressive. Performers are strong as hell. Aerialists, acrobats, whatever. But a lot of feats feel like I've seen done just as well in Cirque du Soleil shows. The bigger problem is the story. Unclear, weak or nonexistent. I left not knowing what it was trying to say. Too much going on at once. Too many visuals, moving pieces, "wow" attempts. A more restrained production would hit harder. Aside from a few cool stunts the whole thing was average. Not blown away. No one I was with seemed overwhelmed either. Some friends did enjoy it. If you've never seen it, maybe check it out. Wynn/Encore deal helps. But I wouldn't see it again. Would not pay full price a second time. It tries to be the stereotypical huge flashy Vegas spectacle. More equals better. More just meant messier for me.

Bought a skateboard at Zumiez recently, went back to buy the rest of the gear. First off it was good vibes, me my friend and his younger brother were chatting with this woman who was putting the board together. Said she was the manager, said she puts boards together every day every day since she got employed. Said when she's having a bad day she gets annoyed and mistreats people or customers. Then it took like 90 mins to assemble despite saying it'll take no more than 15 mins. She stripped two bolts, replaced them in a way that makes it look like she's gonna sell them to another customer or something. Eventually got her brother and another guy, manager, to finish it. No apology. Zumiez lost future business. My heart was crushed.

Snagged it second hand for 38 dollars. Sold it's been a chaotic ride but surprisingly decent. Seller communication was awful. Messaged them before buying about switch type, they took a full week to reply with one word answer, by then I'd already gambled and ordered it. Board itself is in well-loved condition. Spacebar rattles badly, sounds like a loose Lego brick. The E key occasionally repeats itself, makes for some hilarious typos, theee instead of the. But despite the quirks I absolutely love typing on it, tactile feedback fantastic and incredibly comfortable for pounding out long agonizing work emails. Briefly considered shipping it back but returning a 38 dollar heavy slab of plastic is more hassle than its worth so kept it. Grown fond of its flaws. If you don't mind a bit of DIY tuning and a double typing letter now and then, its a budget win.

Travelers, beware Turkish Airlines. Booked Harbin to Beijing domestic flight then Turkish Airlines Beijing to Istanbul. Harbin flight delayed and I missed the connection. At the airport booth nobody took responsibility or helped rebook. Spent the night at airport. Next morning asked for a ticket and staff said flights overbooked, could take days to Istanbul unless I paid for business class. Needed Istanbul so forced to accept. So furious and in disbelief.

bring one broken household item. not more, exactly one. when you get there go to the registration desk and get a number ticket. number decides your queue order. keep the number safe. Repairs by volunteer experts, first come first served. Need to pick up the item before volunteers leave at 4 PM. Anything not claimed they will not store overnight. Need to plan time to wait your turn. We cannot guarantee repair for all devices. Please keep it simple, just follow the rules, smooth ops for everyone here today.

the float valve is how the trough fills. its float drops as the water level drops, opens valve to get water in. water rises so float rises and valve closes gradually. at set level valve shuts off completely. its very common for the float valve to overflow, happens all the time. debris or mineral buildup keeps valve from closing full. or its set to high. float is misadjusted and valve closes after it has already overflowed.

I cant say if food good. We never got to eat. Arrived 7:20pm Sunday. Picked place because 10pm show at same hotel so thought it would be easy. Entered name on digital waitlist, useless thing. Told to come back pay at 8:23pm. We did, waited till 8:40 then they casually say probably not seated till 9:15. Party of two. Zero solutions offered. to all enron employees. difficult days, i know. problems at enron and all the bad stuff in the world, holiday season dont feel like holiday. discussed a lot about going ahead with the all-enron holiday party dec 8. people felt differently, some said good chance to come together and celebrate, others said not appropriate right now. i get both views. given all that happened past month, we cancel the party. spending company funds on celebration right now could be seen as imprudent and we dont want that risk. im sorry, you worked hard, deserve recognition and reason to celebrate, we will find other more suitable ways to recognize your outstanding contributions during holiday season. ken lay

Siphon moves water between two containers over a raised barrier. Works off gravity and air pressure. Tube gets filled so there is one continuous column of water. Gravity drags the water down the long leg to the lower container. So you get a low pressure spot at the top of the siphon. Air pressure pushing on the source water pushes liquid up the short leg into the low pressure spot. That keeps it moving.

Outlet needs to sit below the surface of the source water. Force is the weight diff between water columns on each leg. If the outlet was higher or level with the source, gravity isnt pulling hard enough on the down side to lift on the intake side. Only have net gravitational pull when the outflow column is heavier than the inflow column.

Air in the tube breaks it. The continuous chain of water molecules holds the suction effect. Air bubbles break the cohesion. Air in means pressure inside the tube equals outside. Differential gone and the flow stops. Will not work till you prime it back, fill tube with water again.

The sourdough was on second rise when I found it. Again. It's always Thursday. Always on the flour bin. Always that copy of The Count of Monte Cristo with the Richmond Public Library stamp. I don't know how they get past the squeaky screen door without me hearing. But at 3 AM my brain is mostly yeast and caffeine anyway. Tonight a scrap of yellow legal paper was poking out of the top like a bookmark. I wiped my hands on my apron, left a ghostly white smudge on the dark cloth, pulled it out. Page 142. The note said in frantic spiky handwriting. Please. I think they're watching the drop box now. A cold draft went through the kitchen. Smelled like wet asphalt and oncoming rain. I looked at the darkened front windows. Only my own tired reflection staring back. Didn't open the book. Carefully tucked the note back between the pages, slid the novel into a brown pastry bag, folded the top down twice to seal it.

Picked it up used for $38. Honestly that's all it's worth, maybe a little more.

Flaws first. Space bar rattles every time thumb hits it. Not a click but a hollow loose clatter, like nudging a tray of cutlery. Stopped noticing it during the day but late at night it sounds louder than it has any right to. The E key also repeats itself, so meeting becomes meeeting. Happens once every few paragraphs, just often enough to keep me proofreading. Communication with the seller slow. Asked what switches before buying and the reply came a week after the keyboard had already arrived. Brown switches for the record.

Surprising part is it's genuinely comfortable. Keys have that satisfying cushioned feel, write long emails and wrists don't complain. More than the flat laptop keyboard I was using before. Considered shipping it back but the hassle didn't seem worth it. So it stays on my desk. Rattling, repeating, quietly earning its keep. Three stars.

I was Tom's roommate in a bunk bed until he turned 14. So I have been following his life a long time. The snoring, the fights over the top bunk. And then the early hints of how reliable this guy is. We're celebrating that. Tom is someone you always count on. Forgot my passport once. He made the 6 hour drive to bring it to me. That is the brother, loyal generous one, who will go completely unreasonable distances to save you from your own stupidity. So Tom. I'm very happy you found someone who loves you like we do, and unlike me, decided to room with you on a voluntary basis.

Unbiased rating 4 stars. Personal 2.5 stars. Never wanted to see a Cirque du Soleil before, so Le Reve was my first. I was expecting backflips and some extreme acrobatics and it was a lot less of that and a lot more interpretive dancing than I thought. Performers are very impressive, its just not my thing. People who really like this type of theatre spectacle will probably enjoy Le Reve. But personally I wouldn't pay more than $100 to see shows like these. Luckily I had free tickets and I'm very glad I didn't have to pay.

Old school attendance registers help historians rebuild what daily life looked like, stuff often missing from official accounts. They show up or down, how regular they were, sometimes why they missed school. From that you can guess at seasonal labor, illness, bad weather, poverty, family stuff, migration or local emergencies. You see differences by gender, age, neighborhood, class. Shows how schooling fit into work, home routines, community expectations. If you look across years you can see shifts in schooling habits and public health. Limitation is they only record what the school decided to write. They dont really explain kids experiences, absences could be misreported or incomplete or just what the teacher assumed. So they work best if you cross-reference with other sources.

At 2:17 every Thursday morning the book appears on the bakery back step. Same one always. A Field Guide to North American Moths. County library sticker on the spine is ghost pale. Little flour worked into the jacket, as if the book had been helping out. She returned it twice. The librarians were polite and smiled too hard. By the third week she just left it next to the rye starter. Said nothing.

Tonight rain was ticking on the alley door, ovens breathing. Mara was shaping croissants, palms pushing butter into the dough. Then the latch gave that small guilty click. No one there. Just the book, dry as a bone on wet concrete. She wiped her hands on her apron and opened the book. A folded slip of paper was inside. It was between Luna Moth and Promethea.

Your window is the only light on this street. I read here until the first bus. I’m sorry about the crumbs.

She looked at the alley, dented milk crates, steam rising off the drains. City felt enormous for a second then not. Tore a corner of an order pad and wrote, Cinnamon rolls come out at 4:05. Then put the note inside the book and left it on the warm windowsill and unlocked the back door.

Classroom project, compared folded cardboard bridge stability. Used simple materials controlled tests. Made short beam, arch-inspired, triangular-fold bridges from same cardboard. Tried to keep length width consistent. Bridge placed between two supports, added weights gradually to see bending tipping or collapse. Limited by handmade build, few trials, classroom testing conditions, so dont treat results as engineering data. Triangular folds held weight more steadily in this activity. Fold geometry can influence stability in model bridges.

Marguerite found the book on the steel table by the back door under the bench where the bread peels hang. A Field Guide to Coastal Birds. Inside the cover a Harbor Street branch stamp, due date in March. The mail slot in that door was nailed shut years ago, but the delivery hatch beside it the one the flour man used never latched properly. Eleven Thursdays. She asked day staff, checked the hatch for scratches. Once stayed past four with her coat on. Nothing. The book turned up between two and four and she was always at the ovens her back to the door when it did. Tonight a grocery receipt from Pell's was folded into the page on oystercatchers. Ink blotchy where someone pressed too hard. A note said I keep meaning to take this back to the library. Then I pass your door and there's the smell of bread and I put it down instead. I can stop if you want. She thought whoever it was smelled of salt, because the pages did. Marguerite pulled a pencil from her apron and wrote on the back of the receipt: Bring it Thursday. I'll have a roll. Tucked it in at oystercatchers, set the book on the hatch ledge, put a warm roll in a paper bag beside it.

Now live in Toronto, not using Hydro Ottawa but still want to warn others. Scary billing practices. Had account for a year renting in downtown, moved back home with parents to do an MA. Cancelled account, paid everything owed. But even after cancelling, they kept pulling money from my separate bank account, at random times, over a year. Called customer service multiple times, sent proof of withdrawals. Reps kept saying account closed, no debits. Turns out my parents and I looked at our utility bills and cross-referenced. They linked my banking info to parents' billing number because I said moving home. Parents didn't notice, got overpayment refunds a lot so credits looked normal. Took hours on phone, lots of reps. A manager actually looked into it, confirmed error, fixed it. Weirdly, first they refused refund, only offered apology. Never giving bank details for auto debit again. The way they handle personal data is reckless and everyone should be worried.

3:40am. Second rye batch proofing and Marisol sees that library book again. Flour bin by back door. Plastic jacket cold from alley. Fourth Thursday in a row. Same book, A Field Guide to Night Birds, stamped Eastgate Branch, due three weeks ago. She takes it to drop box on way home every time, every Thursday it comes back like the building borrowed it. Wipes hands on apron opens it. Index card folded, fell out on barn owls page. Card says, you leave the vent fan on, alley smells like bread till five, I walk my mother's dog then, she can't anymore, I keep forgetting to return this, maybe I keep not wanting to, signed R. Marisol read it twice while oven timer counting down. Outside the fan hummed pushing warm air into dark. Flipped card over. With grease pencil she marks trays with, wrote on card, rye's out at 4:15. Tore heel from yesterday's loaf, wrapped in wax paper, put book on top of it, propped back door open one inch.

Ryanair was my way of travelling from England to Sweden where my ex lived, used to be very poor student. Very bad. At airport they confiscated my L’Occitane shower gel, £20 bottle. Said over liquid limit, but it wasn’t. Said go to pharmacy buy 100ml one and it’ll be returned. Did exactly that, came back and nobody had idea what I was on about. Brilliant. £20 gone. Felt very angry. Also at gate they charged me another £5 because I had a bottle of water in carry on. I bought it inside the airport. Ryanair stopped flying from Liverpool John Lennon Airport to Stockholm Skavsta. So now I fly Norwegian Air instead. Customer service poor ironically, but the planes seem newer and less outdated than Ryanair.

I'm no expert but I know what you're describing. I got absolutely soaked on Tuesday and by Thursday half my Brandywines were split open. You can see the seam running down the side of the fruit. Its the same story every year. Dry spell followed by a storm. The flesh absorbs water much faster than the skin can stretch. The Sungolds are mostly doing ok so far. I've got a few looking like they might follow suit. Once it happens you can't really get around it. Keeping your 2 day watering schedule as even as possible helps a bit. But once the sky dumps it all at once that really doesn't matter much. You'll likely get a good crop from the rest of the vines. Pick the split ones off and put them to use in some other way. Its a lot more of a pain with Brandywines. That thick skin is a real liability in a storm. Might get better luck with the Sungolds if you can keep them from getting so much water all at once.

College Board hypocrisy is real. Friend of mine took a one hour SAT subject test and proctor gave room 20 extra min. Her integrity kicked in, knew the extra time messed with standardized part, called official hotline, reported proctor. Then the investigation. They said not enough evidence to hold proctor or other students. But somehow enough to hold my friend. Canceled her scores. So basically the real misconduct goes unpunished, and the honest one gets punished. This is just a broken and unfair system. If you report a test as having a serious issue, and they cancel your score for it, what's the point of even taking tests.

thursdays the book shows up. not on the counter, wedged behind flour bins by the back door, whoever leaves it knows exactly where I won't trip over it. its always same one, A Field Guide to North American Moths from Elmwood Branch, due date stamped so long ago ink gone violet. never seen anyone drop it off. I'm elbow deep in rye dough by 2 and at that hour I wouldn't notice a marching band. first few weeks just set it on shelf by register, by Friday morning gone. Thursday back again. Fine. People are strange. I talk to my sourdough starter, not judging. Tonight there's a note tucked at page 114, the luna moths. They only live a week, they don't even eat. I keep thinking that's a waste of a beautiful thing. Do you ever get to see the bread before its gone. No signature. Just pencil pressed hard. I read it twice then a third time while ovens ticked. Pulled first loaf of the night, still crackling, wrapped in brown paper, set behind flour bins.

Room feels stuffy even when its comfy temp. But temp is just one part of comfort. Humidity, high one, means sweat evaporation from skin slows way down. air feels heavy and stale. Also low airflow matters, no movement and exhaled CO2, odours, heat, they just linger near people and wont disperse. So poor ventilation traps all that stuff and it feels close and oppressive. AC will cool the air but it doesnt necessarily lower humidity or improve circulation. Open window, fan, or run the ventilation and you get a fresher feel. Air moving and moisture going down.

They tell you remote work is a win for everyone. Been mentoring five junior engineers two years now and it isn't. They don't need tickets, docs, scheduled meetings. What they need is to sit in on design arguments, watch someone else work through a nasty bug, get answers before little uncertainty snowballs. You get all that for free in an office. Work from home and they have to figure out when to interrupt, set up a call, explain a problem they probably don't get yet. That's a pretty steep ask for someone who hasn't had the chance to learn it.

I've watched that setup screw up feedback. Short note on a code review ends up reading like final judgment. Lag on getting answers kills forward motion. People I worked with moved ahead way quicker when they could pair up in person, work things out on a whiteboard, actually get hold of the seniors. This isn't to say scrap flexibility. Works fine for people who can direct their own efforts. For a beginner, being around other people is what gets them there. It's how they pick up confidence, context, judgment they're going to need. Hand a newcomer just a laptop and a calendar and you end up with weaker technical leadership down the road.

Rain gauge is simple. You put a tube with an opening of known area, rain falls in. It shows depth, mm or inches. That depth = water covering flat ground with no drainage or evaporation or soak in. Most gauges have a funnel, wide opening, feeds a narrow measuring tube. Same volume of water goes up higher in narrow tube. So you can see tiny amounts more precisely. But the scale is marked with area ratio so it still gives true rainfall depth. Wind is a problem. Wind gusts around it and drops blow past the opening and you get less reading. Also evaporation and splashing before reading, distorts it.

Bought this keyboard used for $38. Fair price, felt right when I pulled it out of the box. Little dust between the keys, some shiny spots on the caps, but not worse than expected for a second hand board. The good part is it is genuinely comfortable. Write long emails for work, hands feel less cramped than on my flat office board. Steady switches, not too heavy, case doesn't slide on desk. Problems though. Space bar rattles every time I hit it, loud enough to notice on quiet mornings. Key e repeats sometimes, type too fast get neeed. Doesn't happen constantly, happens enough to proofread more carefully. Asked seller what switches it has, they answered a full week later, after it already arrived. Not great. Still kept it at $38. Shipping back was more trouble than it was worth.

Bring one broken item per person. Check in at the front table take a numbered ticket. Keep it until your item is returned. Volunteers call numbers in order so stay nearby, some fixes need your input or a quick decision. Not everything can be fixed, parts might need to be ordered, some just not possible. Collect your item before 4:30 p.m. when the volunteers leave. Unclaimed items cant be stored.

Friday around 4:30 p.m. and no line. Two of us hit $130 which felt really expensive. I thought it would be about the same price as a steakhouse, then found out later its actually more than I expected. Disappointed no steak. At that price you expect some kind of steak. They had lamb prime rib and chicken stuff you get at other Vegas buffets for way less. Seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan legs at tons of places but the rock crab claws I hadnt seen anywhere else and that was cool. Problem no crackers for the claws. Staff said wooden mallets available but table was packed right next to next table, didnt want to smash shells and shoot pieces at them. So just ate legs. Asian station wasnt distinctive. Reminded me of Rampart Casino buffet. Dessert had gelato and pastries, nothing stood out. Had fresh juices, didnt try any. Acceptable but overpriced for what you get. If your curious worth trying once if no wait. If the line is long I'd reconsider.

Old attendance registers are huge for historians. Primary sources. They track who showed up. Seasons drive attendance so crops need kids work, flu outbreaks, bad weather. Patterns in attendance tell you about daily rhythms. If its a harvest period, kid has to help farm. If flu hits, attendance drops. If one group consistently misses school, tells you something about social inequality or culture around school. Need to be careful though. The problem is that teachers and headmasters can doctor the numbers. They could be playing games to meet funding requirements or dodge the scrutiny of the authorities. So the data is not always reality. Also registers dont explain why they were missing. You have to go to other sources to work it out, infer causes. These logs give you numbers and a framework to see community dynamics. Everyday life and social structure. But have to cross reference with other evidence.

Apple needs a mention here, personal experience. School only allowed Apple laptops for middle and high school kids, cost about 2x alternatives, broke every month. Never dropped my laptop. Swapped the hard drive 5 times over 4 years, reinstalled os over and over just to keep it running. My friends macbook pro caught fire once. He was watching a movie, smoke alarm went off. Now they put out a new iphone every 2 months or so, camera is slightly better, that’s about it. Credit: ipad is best tablet now. But androids will catch up i think.

Float valves, trough is connected to pressurized water line. A float, usually plastic ball or block, rests on the water surface, attached to lever arm. Cattle drink, level drops, float drops, tilts arm so plunger or washer gets pulled away from seat, water flows into trough. As water rises, float lifts, lever pushes plunger back against seat, narrows opening until flow stops at set level. Overflow happens when washer is worn or has debris on it, can't seal against seat. Also if float is punctured, waterlogged, won't rise enough to close valve.
